query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A low‐temperature aging treatment that induces the formation of coherent L12 nanoprecipitates in the ductile FCC lamella can simultaneously enhance both tensile strength and room‐temperature ductility by reinforcing the phase boundaries and promoting uniform plastic deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies (FCC+B2) having semi‐coherent phase boundaries that act both as dislocation sources and crack initiators.
generation.intervention: Apply a low-temperature aging anneal to trigger the precipitation of coherent, nanoscale L12 particles within the FCC lamella.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation under quasi-static loading conditions with the alloy initially possessing a dual-phase (FCC+B2) lamellar microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: Uniformly distributed, nano-sized coherent L12 precipitates that form within the FCC phase and interact with the existing phase boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The coherent L12 precipitates function as strong, well-bonded obstacles to dislocation motion and pile-up. This increases work hardening by enhancing dislocation storage while simultaneously blunting stress concentrations at the lamellar interfaces. As a result, both strength is increased (via Orowan-type dislocation bowing and barrier strengthening) and ductility is improved (by delaying microcrack initiation and propagation).
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast lamellar-colony baseline, the low-temperature aged alloy will exhibit higher yield and tensile strengths and an increased room-temperature elongation, due to improved dislocation interactions and a more homogeneously deforming microstructure.
generation.baseline: The unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloy with its as-cast dual-phase lamellar structure, where phase boundaries are semi-coherent and prone to microcracking under tensile loads.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective provided that the aging treatment promotes a uniform and fine dispersion of coherent L12 precipitates without coarsening or dissolving critical phase boundary features. Its success depends on maintaining the delicate balance between reinforcing phase boundaries and preserving adequate ductile matrix connectivity in alloys with similar dual-phase lamellar morphologies.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements in strength and ductility are uncertain, as they depend on the extent, size, and distribution of the L12 precipitates. Moreover, the interplay between precipitate-induced strengthening and potential changes in phase boundary chemistry requires further validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the eutectic high-entropy alloy: one batch is subjected to a low-temperature aging treatment tailored to induce L12 nanoprecipitation while the other is retained in the as-cast condition. Characterize both batches using TEM to confirm the presence or absence of coherent L12 precipitates and assess phase-boundary integrity. Perform quasi-static room-temperature tensile tests to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation. Compare the mechanical performance of the treated samples with that of the untreated baseline.
measurements: TEM microstructural analysis (precipitate size, density, and coherence)
Room-temperature tensile strength (yield and ultimate stresses)
Dislocation storage and work hardening rates (from stress-strain curves)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the as-cast baseline, or if the anticipated coherent L12 nanoprecipitates are not observed via TEM, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The properties of many metallic alloys are essentially related to the structure, morphology and chemical distribution of boundaries. In terms of atomic structure, the phase boundaries contained in eutectic dual-phase HEAs were supposed to be insufficient in prohibiting dislocations due to their semi-coherent nature, which is similar to those widely reported in NiAl dual-phase intermetallic alloys,. However, in-situ deformation tests revealed that dense dislocation storage can be achieved within FCC phases and dislocation walls were formed along phase boundaries. The unexpected strong interfaces are thought to be highly related to the chemically disordered distribution of multiple solution atoms at phase boundaries as well as in the matrix of HEAs. Particularly, an ultra-thin segregation zone of randomly distributed Cr atoms, typically less than 2 nm in width (Fig. 3b and S4), was detected near the phase boundary without forming complex intermetallic compounds, which were intrinsically brittle and would lead to stress concentration. Recent studies indicate that eutectic high-entropy alloys can simultaneously possess high strength and high ductility, which have potential industrial applications. The present study focuses on Al0.7CoCrFeNi, a lamellar dual-phase (fcc + B2) precipitation-strengthenable eutectic high entropy alloy. This alloy exhibits an fcc + B2 (B2 with bcc nano-precipitates) microstructure resulting in a combination of the soft and ductile fcc phase together with hard B2 phase. Low temperature annealing leads to the precipitation of ordered L12 intermetallic precipitates within the fcc resulting in enhanced strength. The strengthening contribution due to fine scale L12 is modeled using Orowan dislocation bowing and by-pass mechanism. The alloy was tested under quasi-static (strain-rate = 10−3 s−1) tensile loading and dynamic (strain-rate = 103 s−1) compressive loading. Due to the fine lamellar microstructure with a large number of fcc-bcc interfaces, the alloy show relatively high flow-stresses, ~1400 MPa under quasi-static loading and in excess of 1800 MPa under dynamic loading.
